steps.title: Amarone and Recioto
steps.body: Recioto della Valpolicella is the oldest style: dried grapes fermented to leave sweetness. Amarone della Valpolicella, DOCG since 2010, is fermented almost dry, reaching 15 to 16% alcohol. Amarone means the big bitter one, compared with Recioto's sweetness. Legend says it was born when a Recioto fermented too far.

steps.title: Ripasso
steps.body: Ripasso, meaning re-passed, is made by refermenting young Valpolicella on the leftover skins of Amarone or Recioto. The skins add sugar, colour, tannin and dried fruit flavour, plus a few degrees of alcohol. The result sits between simple Valpolicella and Amarone, sometimes called baby Amarone.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of making a Ripasso in order.
steps.explanation: Ripasso borrows the skins left after Amarone is pressed, so Amarone comes first.

steps.title: Ageing Amarone
steps.body: Amarone must age at least two years from January after harvest; Riserva at least four. Traditionally, it aged in large Slavonian oak casks; many producers now use French barriques. Producers like Quintarelli and Dal Forno made it famous worldwide.

options: By drying grapes for six months
By refermenting Valpolicella on Amarone skins
steps.explanation: The leftover skins add body and flavour.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Recioto is sweet; Amarone is dry and powerful, at 15 to 16%
Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on Amarone skins
Amarone ages at least two years; Riserva four
